hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=-3\sqrt{x-1}+2$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=-3\sqrt{x-1}+2$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt{x}\\\\
f(x-1)&=\sqrt{x-1}\\\\
-3f(x-1)&=-3\sqrt{x-1}\\\\
-3f(x-1)+2&=-3\sqrt{x-1}+2
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $-g(x)=3f(x-1)+2$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x-1$ shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ to the right $1$ unit.

[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A square root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint at (zero, zero) and passes through (four, two). The shifted graph has an endpoint at (one, zero) and passes through (five, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $\sqrt{x-1}$ by $-3$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}$ across the $x$-axis and stretches it vertically by a factor of $3$.

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that the graph of the function passes through $(5,2)$ *before* the transformation, and $(5, -6 )$ *after* the transformation.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $-3$.

options.alt: A square root function graph and its transformed graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint at (one, zero) and passes through (five, two). The transformed graph has an endpoint at (one, zero) and passes through (five, negative six).

hints.content:
Adding $2$ to the function shifts the graph of $y=-3\sqrt{x-1}$ up $2$ units.

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 2]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, two) and passes through (ten, negative one).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/838d19b306cd3a25ac6c67be671bb6a26eaf0e71)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/76bbee52d28bfb5f5bcd72a6831a797eaab9824d)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

options.alt: A square root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint at (one, zero) and passes through (five, negative six). The shifted graph has an endpoint at (one, two) and passes through (five, negative four).
